claim: Loss of mammalian Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) accompanies progression to invasive urothelial carcinoma.
source: In bladder, loss of mammalian Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) accompanies progression to invasive urothelial carcinoma, but the molecular mechanisms underlying this cancer-initiating event are poorly defined.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established observation that motivates the study.

claim: Loss of Shh results from hypermethylation of the CpG shore of the Shh gene.
source: Here, we show that loss of Shh results from hypermethylation of the CpG shore of the Shh gene
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibition of DNA methylation increases Shh expression.
source: inhibition of DNA methylation increases Shh expression to halt the initiation of murine urothelial carcinoma at the early stage of progression
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and 1F showing increased Shh expression upon 5'-azacitidine treatment.

claim: Inhibition of DNA methylation halts the initiation of murine urothelial carcinoma at the early stage of progression.
source: inhibition of DNA methylation increases Shh expression to halt the initiation of murine urothelial carcinoma at the early stage of progression
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data in Figure 1H showing absence of invasive carcinoma with 5'-azacitidine treatment.

claim: Pharmacologic augmentation of Hedgehog pathway activity impedes tumor growth in full-fledged tumors.
source: In full-fledged tumors, pharmacologic augmentation of Hedgehog (Hh) pathway activity impedes tumor growth
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2 showing reduced tumor growth with 5'-azacitidine treatment.

claim: The cancer-restraining effect of Hh signaling is mediated by the stromal response to Shh signals.
source: this cancer-restraining effect of Hh signaling is mediated by the stromal response to Shh signals
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic ablation experiments in Figures 1J-K and 2D-E showing loss of anticancer effect when stromal Hh response is blocked.

claim: Hh signaling stimulates subtype conversion of basal to luminal-like urothelial carcinoma.
source: this cancer-restraining effect of Hh signaling is mediated by the stromal response to Shh signals, which stimulates subtype conversion of basal to luminal-like urothelial carcinoma
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining and gene expression data in Figures 4 and 5 showing increased luminal markers with 5'-azacitidine treatment.

claim: Hedgehog signaling has post-embryonic roles in homeostatic maintenance of tissue integrity.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) signaling has been recognized for its post-embryonic roles in the homeostatic maintenance of tissue integrity and the development of human malignancies (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Goodrich et al., 1997; Shin et al., 2011; Taipale and Beachy, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hedgehog signaling has post-embryonic roles in the development of human malignancies.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) signaling has been recognized for its post-embryonic roles in the homeostatic maintenance of tissue integrity and the development of human malignancies (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Goodrich et al., 1997; Shin et al., 2011; Taipale and Beachy, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The first FDA-approved drug targeting the Hh pathway was developed for treatment of human malignancy.
source: The initial identification of Hh pathway activity in human cancers, including basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma, has led to the development of the first FDA-approved drug targeting the Hh pathway for the treatment of human malignancy (Goodrich et al., 1997; Ruch and Kim, 2013; Sekulic et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hh pathway antagonism is not beneficial in pancreatic, colon or ovarian cancers.
source: Despite promising early preclinical studies (Olive et al., 2009; Yauch et al., 2008), recent studies investigating pancreatic, colon or ovarian cancers have shown that Hh pathway antagonism is not beneficial and clinical trials had to be halted in some cases because of accelerated cancer growth (Herter-Sprie et al., 2013; Kaye et al., 2012; Ruch and Kim, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hh pathway activity has a protective role in progression of cancers originating from endodermally derived tissues.
source: Consistent with the results of human trials, several recent studies have shown a protective role of Hh pathway activity in the progression of cancers that originate from endodermally derived tissues, including the bladder (Shin et al., 2014a; Shin et al., 2014b), pancreas (Lee et al., 2014; Rhim et al., 2014), colon (Gerling et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016), and prostate (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The tumor-restraining effect of Hh signaling is exerted by the stromal response to Hh signals from epithelial cancer cells.
source: This tumor-restraining effect on a wide range of solid cancers is suggested to be exerted by the stromal response to Hh signals elicited from epithelial cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature and the authors' interpretation.

claim: In the bladder, the Hh response is restricted to the stroma.
source: In the bladder, an organ of endodermal origin, the Hh response is restricted to the stroma while Sonic hedgehog (Shh) protein is produced in basal epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Shin et al., 2011).

claim: Sonic hedgehog (Shh) protein is produced in basal epithelial cells in the bladder.
source: In the bladder, an organ of endodermal origin, the Hh response is restricted to the stroma while Sonic hedgehog (Shh) protein is produced in basal epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Shin et al., 2011).

claim: The regulatory circuit involving Hh signaling feedback between bladder epithelium and stroma is required for proliferative response to injury during urothelial regeneration.
source: The regulatory circuit involving Hh signaling feedback between the bladder epithelium and supporting stromal cells is required for the proliferative response to injury during urothelial regeneration (Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Shh expression is lost during the development of invasive urothelial carcinoma.
source: Surprisingly, Shh expression is lost during the development of invasive urothelial carcinoma, even though the tumor is derived from Shh-expressing stem cells (Shin et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Invasive urothelial carcinoma is derived from Shh-expressing stem cells.
source: Surprisingly, Shh expression is lost during the development of invasive urothelial carcinoma, even though the tumor is derived from Shh-expressing stem cells (Shin et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Genetic ablation of Hh signal response in stromal cells accelerates tumor progression at an early stage.
source: genetic ablation of Hh signal response in stromal cells accelerates tumor progression at an early stage (Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of Shh expression invariably accompanies progression to invasive carcinoma.
source: These studies have shown that loss of Shh expression invariably accompanies progression to invasive carcinoma
evidence: This is based on cited previous studies.

claim: Suppression of the Hh response in tumor stroma significantly accelerates the initiation of cancer.
source: suppression of the Hh response in the tumor stroma significantly accelerates the initiation of cancer
evidence: This is based on cited previous studies.

claim: Hh pathway activity protects against tumor progression at early stages of tumor development.
source: Hh pathway activity protects against tumor progression at early stages of tumor development
evidence: This is an inference based on cited previous studies.

claim: Mutations of genes involved in epigenetic regulation are highly enriched in invasive urothelial carcinomas.
source: Interestingly, recent large-scale genomic studies in human bladder cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014a) have revealed that mutations of genes involved in epigenetic regulation are highly enriched in invasive urothelial carcinomas
evidence: This is supported by citation to TCGA study.

claim: There are no mutational changes in the SHH gene in invasive urothelial carcinomas.
source: while an extensive analysis by our group showed no mutational changes in the SHH gene
evidence: This is supported by the authors' analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Epigenetic activities may be responsible for the loss of SHH expression during the initiation of urothelial carcinomas.
source: these results raise the possibility that epigenetic activities may be responsible for the loss of SHH expression during the initiation of urothelial carcinomas
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of enriched epigenetic mutations and lack of SHH mutations.

claim: Recent large-scale genomic studies revealed five distinct subtypes of bladder cancer.
source: Recent large-scale genomic studies of gene expression in human urothelial carcinoma have revealed five distinct subtypes of bladder cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014a; Choi et al., 2014; Robertson et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interactions between epithelial cancer cells and tumor stroma are important for initiation and growth of human cancers.
source: Interactions between epithelial cancer cells and the tumor stroma are important for the initiation and growth of human cancers (Calon et al., 2015; Isella et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hh signaling to the stroma induces the expression of Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs).
source: Our previous work has shown that Hh signaling to the stroma induces the expression of Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which impede bladder cancer progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Shin et al., 2014b).

claim: BMPs impede bladder cancer progression.
source: Our previous work has shown that Hh signaling to the stroma induces the expression of Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which impede bladder cancer progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Shin et al., 2014b).

claim: The anti-cancer effect of Hh-induced stromal BMPs is mediated by urothelial differentiation of pre-cancerous cells at the early stage of tumor initiation.
source: This anti-cancer effect of Hh-induced stromal expression of BMPs is mediated by urothelial differentiation of pre-cancerous cells at the early stage of tumor initiation (Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DNA methylation at the CpG shore upstream of the CpG island of the Shh promoter region is significantly increased in murine invasive urothelial carcinomas compared to wild-type bladders.
source: By performing bisulfite sequencing analysis, we found significant increases in DNA methylation at the CpG shore upstream of the CpG island of the Shh promoter region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) in murine invasive urothelial carcinomas compared to that in wild-type bladders (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of DNA methyltransferase activity with 5'-azacitidine in BBN-induced urothelial carcinoma decreased the level of DNA methylation.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) activity with 5'-azacitidine in BBN-induced urothelial carcinoma decreased the level of DNA methylation (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: 5'-azacitidine treatment significantly increases the expression of Shh in BBN-induced urothelial carcinoma.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) activity with 5'-azacitidine in BBN-induced urothelial carcinoma decreased the level of DNA methylation (Figure 1A,B), with significant increases in the expression of Shh (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C showing 11-fold increase.

claim: Bladder tumor organoids derived from BBN-induced urothelial carcinoma can recapitulate the pathology of the original tumors.
source: Orthotopic transplantation of these tumor organoids revealed the histopathology of parental tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that these organoids could recapitulate the pathology of the original BBN-induced urothelial carcinomas.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The CpG shore of the Shh promoter region in bladder tumor organoids is hypermethylated.
source: Consistent with the results from BBN-induced tumors, our analyses revealed that the CpG shore of the Shh promoter region in bladder tumor organoids were also hypermethylated
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Treatment with 5'-azacitidine decreases methylation level in bladder tumor organoids.
source: following the treatment of 5'-azacitidine, the level of methylation was decreased (Figure 1D,E)
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Treatment with 5'-azacitidine significantly increases the expression of Shh in bladder tumor organoids.
source: following the treatment of 5'-azacitidine, the level of methylation was decreased (Figure 1D,E), with significant increases in the expression of Shh (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F showing 9-fold increase.

claim: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) becomes robust and widespread when mice are exposed to BBN for 4 months.
source: As previously established (Shin et al., 2014a), carcinoma in situ (CIS) became robust and widespread when mice were exposed to BBN for 4 months.
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: Widespread CIS contains premalignant cells with Shh expression.
source: This widespread CIS contains premalignant cells with Shh expression and represents a precursor lesion in muscle-invasive carcinoma.
evidence: This is based on previous work and the authors' characterization.

claim: BBN exposure for a total of 6 months results in the development of invasive carcinoma.
source: Without 5'-azacitidine treatment, BBN exposure for a total of 6 months resulted in the development of invasive carcinoma (Shin et al., 2014a; Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work and supported by histological data in Figure 1H.

claim: No invasive carcinoma was observed in mice treated with 5'-azacitidine during the final 2 months of BBN exposure.
source: whereas no invasive carcinoma was observed in mice treated with 5'-azacitidine during the final 2 months (Figure 1H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Inhibition of DNA methylation impedes tumor initiation if treatment is administered prior to the formation of invasive carcinoma.
source: suggesting that inhibition of DNA methylation impeded tumor initiation if treatment was administered prior to the formation of invasive carcinoma
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no invasive carcinoma with 5'-azacitidine treatment.

claim: The antitumor initiation effect of 5'-azacitidine was reversed when the Hh response in the stroma was genetically ablated.
source: In mice treated with TM to ablate the Hh response in the stroma, we found that the antitumor initiation effect of 5'-azacitidine was reversed and that invasive carcinomas appeared at 6 months, as in normal BBN-exposed mice, whereas no invasive carcinoma was observed in control animals (Figure 1J,K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 1J, 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: DNA methylation of the Shh gene functions as a molecular basis for the loss of Shh expression in invasive urothelial carcinoma.
source: These findings suggested that DNA methylation of the Shh gene functions as a molecular basis for the loss of Shh expression in invasive urothelial carcinoma
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing hypermethylation and loss of Shh expression.

claim: Hh signaling to the stroma plays a role in the initiation of bladder cancer at the early stage of disease.
source: confirmed the role of Hh signaling to the stroma in the initiation of bladder cancer at the early stage of disease, as previously reported (Shin et al., 2014a; Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is confirmed by the rescue experiments and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of DNA methylation fully impedes the growth of bladder tumors in immunocompetent wild-type animals.
source: In bladders from 5'-azacitidine-treated mice, however, no invasive carcinoma was observed (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that inhibition of DNA methylation fully impeded the growth of bladder tumors in immunocompetent wild-type animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The anticancer propagation effect of 5'-azacitidine is mediated by the stromal Hh response.
source: In both strains with genetic ablation of the stromal Hh response, the anticancer growth effect of 5'-azacitidine disappeared (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The effect of 5'-azacitidine on tumor cell propagation is mediated through the stromal Hh response elicited by Shh.
source: These results strongly suggested that the effect of 5'-azacitidine on the propagation of tumor cells was mediated through the stromal Hh response elicited by Shh, whose expression is regulated epigenetically by cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic ablation experiments showing loss of anticancer effect when stromal Hh response is blocked.

claim: BMPs are secreted stromal factors for urothelial differentiation.
source: Bmps are secreted stromal factors for urothelial differentiation (Mysorekar et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: BMP pathway activity impedes bladder cancer progression prior to the formation of invasive carcinoma by stimulating urothelial differentiation.
source: BMP pathway activity impedes bladder cancer progression prior to the formation of invasive carcinoma by stimulating urothelial differentiation (Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bmp4-expressing tumor organoids showed growth reductions after transplantation compared with wild-type bladder tumor organoids.
source: We found that, compared with wild-type bladder tumor organoids, Bmp4-expressing tumor organoids showed growth reductions after transplantation (Figure 3B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 3B, 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Bmp4-treated organoids grew slowly and the efficiency of organoid formation was significantly reduced.
source: after tumor organoids were cultured in the presence of the Bmp4 protein to increase the BMP response (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), the Bmp4-treated organoids grew slowly, and the efficiency of organoid formation was significantly reduced (Figure 3D,E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by organoid culture data shown in Figure 3D, 3E, and 3F.

claim: Hypomethylation-induced Shh secretion by tumor cells activates the Hh response in bladder stroma, resulting in stromal expression of Bmps, which signal back to tumor cells to impede their growth.
source: Taken together, the tumor-suppressing effect of Bmp, particularly in vivo where tumor cells still express Shh (with 5'-azacitidine treatment) while the stromal Hh response is suppressed (using Col1a2CreER;Smoflox/flox and Col1a2CreER;Gli2flox/flox mice), supports a potential scenario of an increased reciprocal tumor-stromal signal feedback loop in which hypomethylation-induced Shh secretion by tumor cells activates the Hh response in bladder stroma, resulting in stromal expression of Bmps, which in turn signal back to tumor cells to impede their growth.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Transplanted bladder tumors in nude mice grew even under 5'-azacitidine treatment, but gave rise to tumor lesions with smaller sizes than those without 5'-azacitidine treatment.
source: Indeed, transplanted bladder tumors in nude mice grew even under 5'-azacitidine treatment, but they gave rise to tumor lesions with smaller sizes than those without 5'-azacitidine treatment (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: 5'-azacitidine treatment is effective in suppressing tumor growth under immunocompromised conditions.
source: These findings suggest that 5'-azacitidine treatment is still effective in suppressing tumor growth under immunocompromised conditions, which is consistent with our earlier results (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced tumor size with 5'-azacitidine treatment in nude mice.

claim: BBN-induced invasive carcinomas are most similar to the basal subtype of human urothelial carcinoma.
source: As previously reported (Fantini et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2014b), based on the expression level of basal markers and mutational profile, the invasive carcinomas produced in our BBN model are most similar to the basal subtype of human urothelial carcinoma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The basal subtype of bladder cancer is the most aggressive form.
source: the invasive carcinomas produced in our BBN model are most similar to the basal subtype of human urothelial carcinoma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), which is the most aggressive form of bladder cancer (Choi et al., 2014; Vasconcelos-Nóbrega et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The expression of the luminal marker Ck18 was increased in tumors treated with 5'-azacitidine.
source: Our immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the expression of the luminal marker, Ck18, was increased in the tumors treated with 5'-azacitidine, while control bladders displayed basal phenotypes such as squamous differentiation and the expression of Ck5, a marker for the basal subtype (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D, 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Control bladders displayed basal phenotypes such as squamous differentiation and the expression of Ck5.
source: Our immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the expression of the luminal marker, Ck18, was increased in the tumors treated with 5'-azacitidine, while control bladders displayed basal phenotypes such as squamous differentiation and the expression of Ck5, a marker for the basal subtype (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D, 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The expression level of luminal markers relative to basal markers was significantly increased in transplanted bladder tumors under 5'-azacitidine treatment.
source: Moreover, our quantitative RT-PCR experiments showed that the expression level of luminal markers relative to basal markers was significantly increased in the transplanted bladder tumors under 5'-azacitidine treatment compared with that of the control group, which was accompanied by increased expression of Shh (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Tumors orthotopically grown in the presence of 5'-azacitidine showed strong luminal signature with relatively low expression of basal markers.
source: Consistent with these results, our analysis of RNA-seq expression profiles revealed the strong luminal signature with relatively low expression of basal markers in the tumors orthotopically grown in the presence of 5'-azacitidine, whereas control allografts in the absence of 5'-azacitidine showed clear standard signature of basal subtype (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) (Damrauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Control allografts in the absence of 5'-azacitidine showed clear standard signature of basal subtype.
source: Consistent with these results, our analysis of RNA-seq expression profiles revealed the strong luminal signature with relatively low expression of basal markers in the tumors orthotopically grown in the presence of 5'-azacitidine, whereas control allografts in the absence of 5'-azacitidine showed clear standard signature of basal subtype (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) (Damrauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Subtype conversion between basal and luminal-like subtypes resulting from increased Hh response might account for reduced tumor growth.
source: These results suggested that subtype conversion between basal and luminal-like subtypes resulting from the increased Hh response induced by epigenetically upregulated expression of Shh in tumor cells might account for the reduced tumor growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing subtype conversion and reduced tumor growth.

claim: The expression levels of luminal markers were significantly decreased in tumor organoids following the expression of shRNA targeting Shh after transplantation.
source: The expression levels of luminal markers were significantly decreased in tumor organoids following the expression of the shRNA targeting Shh after transplantation, indicating the basal-like characteristics including squamous differentiation of the resulting tumors, even under 5'-azacitidine treatment (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological and gene expression data shown in Figure 5B, 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Tumors expressing shRNA for Shh showed basal-like characteristics including squamous differentiation even under 5'-azacitidine treatment.
source: The expression levels of luminal markers were significantly decreased in tumor organoids following the expression of the shRNA targeting Shh after transplantation, indicating the basal-like characteristics including squamous differentiation of the resulting tumors, even under 5'-azacitidine treatment (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological and gene expression data shown in Figure 5B, 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The gene signature related with luminal status is negatively enriched in tumors expressing shRNA for Shh.
source: Consistent with these results, our analysis of RNA-seq expression profiles confirmed that the gene signature related with the luminal status is negatively enriched in the tumors expressing shRNA for Shh, whereas tumor expressing control shRNA showed standard signature of luminal-like subtype (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: mCherry-labeled tumors expressing shRNA for Shh developed into a more aggressive, rapidly growing basal-like subtype, whereas EGFP-labeled control tumors developed into a less aggressive luminal-like subtype in the same microenvironment.
source: The resulting allografts revealed that mCherry-labeled tumors developed into a more aggressive, rapidly growing basal-like subtype, whereas, in the same microenvironment, EGFP-labeled tumors developed into a less aggressive luminal-like subtype following treatment with 5'-azacitidine (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Transplantation of Bmpr1a knock-down tumor organoids in the presence of 5'-azacitidine gave rise to secondary tumors with decreased expression of luminal markers with squamous differentiation.
source: transplantation of Bmpr1a knock-down tumor organoids in the presence of 5'-azacitidine gave rise to secondary tumors with decreased expression of luminal markers with squamous differentiation compared to tumor organoids with intact Bmpr1a (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological and gene expression data shown in Figure 5B, 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,E.

claim: The gene signature related with luminal status is negatively enriched in tumors expressing shRNA for Bmpr1a.
source: Consistent with these results, our analysis of RNA-seq expression profiles confirmed that the gene signature related with the luminal status is negatively enriched in the tumors expressing shRNA for Bmpr1a (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: mCherry-labeled tumors expressing shRNA for Bmpr1a developed into a more rapidly growing basal-like subtype than EGFP-labeled tumors with luminal-like subtype, even under 5'-azacitidine treatment.
source: The mixed allografts showed that mCherry-labeled tumors developed into a more rapidly growing basal-like subtype than EGFP-labeled tumors with the luminal-like subtype, even under 5'-azacitidine treatment (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Organoids with genetic ablation of Bmpr1a developed into basal invasive carcinoma, even with 5'-azacitidine treatment.
source: Consistent with the findings described above, the resulting organoids developed into basal invasive carcinoma, even with 5'-azacitidine treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Subtype conversion between basal and luminal-like subtypes depends on reciprocal signaling feedback between tumor cells and stroma involving epigenetically regulated epithelial Hh expression, stromal Hh response-induced Bmp expression, and BMP response in tumor cells.
source: Taken together, our results from various genetic experiments in combination with pharmacological approaches to manipulate Hh and BMP signaling feedback during the growth of bladder tumors strongly suggest that subtype conversion between basal and luminal-like subtypes depends on the reciprocal signaling feedback between tumor cells and the stroma involving epigenetically regulated epithelial Hh expression in tumor cells, stromal Hh response-induced Bmp expression, and the BMP response in tumor cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental data from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: All three human bladder cancer cell lines (J82, T24, TCC-SUP) showed a significant increase in DNA methylation at the CpG shore of the SHH promoter region.
source: Consistent with our mouse experiments described above (Figure 1), all three cell lines showed a significant increase in DNA methylation at the CpG shore of the SHH promoter region (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6A, 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Human bladder cancer cell lines J82, T24, and TCC-SUP demonstrate basal characteristics of urothelial carcinoma with low levels of SHH expression.
source: all three cell lines showed a significant increase in DNA methylation at the CpG shore of the SHH promoter region (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and demonstrated basal characteristics of urothelial carcinoma with low levels of SHH expression.
evidence: This is a characterization based on the methylation and expression data.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT activity with 5'-azacitidine in human bladder cancer cell lines significantly decreased the level of DNA methylation.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT activity with 5'-azacitidine in these cell lines significantly decreased the level of DNA methylation (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: 5'-azacitidine treatment was associated with marked increases in the expression of SHH in human bladder cancer cell lines.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT activity with 5'-azacitidine in these cell lines significantly decreased the level of DNA methylation (Figure 6A,B), which was associated with marked increases in the expression of SHH (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C showing 6-fold, 7-fold, and 3-fold increases.

claim: Inhibition of DNA methylation inhibits the growth of human bladder tumor.
source: In bladders from 5'-azacitidine treated mice, however, much smaller lesions were observed (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that inhibition of DNA methylation inhibited the growth of human bladder tumor.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Xenografts from 5'-azacitidine-treated animals showed characteristics of the luminal-like subtype, with increased expression of luminal markers.
source: In addition, xenografts from 5'-azacitidine-treated animals showed characteristics of the luminal-like subtype, with increased expression of luminal markers (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The expression levels of basal markers were significantly increased in human bladder cancer xenografts with shRNA targeting SHH or BMPR1A, even upon 5'-azacitidine treatment.
source: After transplantation, the resulting tumors maintained a low level of SHH or BMPR1A expression (Figure 6H), and the expression levels of basal markers were significantly increased, with low expression levels of luminal markers being observed even upon 5'-azacitidine treatment (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6H and 6I.

claim: The Hh pathway response in tumor stroma induced by elevated expression of Hh in tumor cells impedes the growth of bladder cancer through stromal BMP-induced subtype conversion.
source: These human data are consistent with our observations in the mouse model, showing that the Hh pathway response in the tumor stroma induced by elevated expression of Hh in tumor cells impedes the growth of bladder cancer through stromal BMP-induced subtype conversion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the human xenograft data consistent with mouse model findings.

claim: Six invasive carcinoma samples from patients showed characteristics of the basal subtype, with the expression of basal markers being significantly increased.
source: We found that the invasive carcinoma samples from six patients showed characteristics of the basal subtype, with the expression of basal markers being significantly increased (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four invasive carcinoma samples from patients exhibited a luminal phenotype, with elevated expression of luminal markers.
source: The invasive carcinoma samples from the remaining four patients exhibited a luminal phenotype, with elevated expression of luminal markers (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The luminal phenotype of human primary bladder cancer samples was accompanied by a marked increase in the expression of SHH.
source: Consistent with the data from our BBN model and human bladder cancer cell lines (Figures 4 and 6), the luminal phenotype of the human primary bladder cancer samples was accompanied by a marked increase in the expression of SHH, whereas human primary tumors with the basal phenotype showed a significant decrease in SHH expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Human primary tumors with the basal phenotype showed a significant decrease in SHH expression.
source: Consistent with the data from our BBN model and human bladder cancer cell lines (Figures 4 and 6), the luminal phenotype of the human primary bladder cancer samples was accompanied by a marked increase in the expression of SHH, whereas human primary tumors with the basal phenotype showed a significant decrease in SHH expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The methylation of the SHH gene, especially in the CpG shore of the promoter region, was significantly increased in the basal subtype of human invasive carcinomas compared to benign urothelia.
source: We found that the methylation of the SHH gene, especially in the CpG shore of the promoter region, was significantly increased in the basal subtype of human invasive carcinomas compared to that in benign urothelia (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Decreased methylation in luminal subtypes of invasive carcinoma relative to basal subtypes was observed in human samples.
source: Decreased methylation in luminal subtypes of invasive carcinoma relative to basal subtypes was also observed in these human samples (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: The patient group with high SHH expression survived for a median of 50 months, compared to 39 months in the group with low SHH expression.
source: We found that the group with high SHH expression survived for a median of 50 months, compared to 39 months in the group with low SHH expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from survival analysis of 41 patients shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The patient group with higher SHH expression had better patient outcomes, presenting a 28% survival benefit compared to the group with lower SHH expression.
source: The patient group with higher SHH expression therefore had better patient outcomes, presenting a 28% survival benefit compared to the group with lower SHH expression (log rank test p<0.05, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from survival analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The group with low SHH expression showed molecular characteristics of the basal subtype with poor patient outcomes compared to the high-SHH group with luminal characteristics.
source: We noted that the group with low SHH expression showed molecular characteristics of the basal subtype with poor patient outcomes compared to those of the high-SHH group with luminal characteristics (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The basal cluster showed the lowest level of SHH expression.
source: We noted that the basal cluster showed the lowest level of SHH expression (Figure 7F), consistent with our previous analysis and results from other studies (Robertson et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is a primary finding from TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 7F and supported by citations.

claim: The median overall survival of patients with the basal subtype was significantly lower than that of patients with the luminal subtype.
source: the median overall survival of patients with the basal subtype was significantly lower than that of patients with the luminal subtype (log rank test p<0.0001, Figure 7G)
evidence: This is a primary finding from TCGA data survival analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Only a small fraction of patients carried genetic mutations in SHH and its downstream genes.
source: It is important to note that only a small fraction of the patients carried genetic mutations in SHH and its downstream genes, suggesting that genetic alterations might not have been the major cause of the loss of SHH expression signatures in human invasive bladder cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genetic alterations might not have been the major cause of the loss of SHH expression signatures in human invasive bladder cancer.
source: It is important to note that only a small fraction of the patients carried genetic mutations in SHH and its downstream genes, suggesting that genetic alterations might not have been the major cause of the loss of SHH expression signatures in human invasive bladder cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the low frequency of genetic mutations in SHH pathway genes.

claim: Loss of SHH expression due to hypermethylation leads to decreased expression of stromal BMP, which stimulates formation of the basal subtype of human bladder cancer with poor clinical outcomes.
source: Taken together, our findings from extensive analyses of primary tumor samples and a TCGA dataset suggest a possible basis for the development of the basal subtype of human invasive carcinomas that lack active Hh signaling. Under this scenario, loss of SHH expression due to hypermethylation leads to the decreased expression of stromal BMP, which in turn stimulates the formation of the basal subtype of human bladder cancer, with poor clinical outcomes.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the comprehensive analysis of patient samples and TCGA data.

claim: Clonal loss of Shh expression caused by DNA methylation leads to suppression of the stromal Hh response.
source: Following the formation of widespread CIS, the clonal loss of Shh expression caused by DNA methylation leads to suppression of the stromal Hh response
evidence: This is part of the proposed model summarized in the Discussion and Figure 8.

claim: Suppression of the stromal Hh response increases the number of undifferentiated premalignant cells with proliferative advantages due to decreased expression of stromal differentiation factors.
source: the clonal loss of Shh expression caused by DNA methylation leads to suppression of the stromal Hh response, which in turn increases the number of undifferentiated premalignant cells with proliferative advantages due to the decreased expression of stromal differentiation factors.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model summarized in the Discussion and Figure 8.

claim: The critical event of Shh loss facilitates the initiation and progression of tumors at early stages, ultimately resulting in formation of the Shh-negative, basal subtype of invasive carcinoma.
source: This critical event facilitates the initiation and progression of tumors at early stages, ultimately resulting in the formation of the Shh-negative, basal subtype of invasive carcinoma.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model summarized in the Discussion and Figure 8.

claim: Once formed, the basal subtype of urothelial carcinoma remains Shh negative.
source: Once formed, the basal subtype of urothelial carcinoma remains Shh negative, consistent with the observed loss of Shh in murine and human invasive urothelial carcinoma with basal characteristics (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014a; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014b; Shin et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Invasive urothelial carcinoma of the luminal subtype develops through the distinct papillary lineage, as Shh expression is maintained.
source: In contrast, invasive urothelial carcinoma of the luminal subtype develops through the distinct papillary lineage, as Shh expression is maintained, with a low CIS mutational profile.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model summarized in the Discussion and Figure 8.

claim: A luminal-like subtype can be induced from the basal subtype of urothelial carcinoma by pharmacological modulation with 5'-azacitidine.
source: One key feature of our model is that a luminal-like subtype can be induced from the basal subtype of urothelial carcinoma by pharmacological modulation with 5'-azacitidine, to increase the expression of Shh in tumor cells, resulting in an increased stromal Hh response.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The Hh-dependent conversion of tumor subtypes is likely mediated by stromal Bmps.
source: The Hh-dependent conversion of tumor subtypes is likely mediated by stromal Bmps, as supported by our observation that increased Bmp expression in tumor cells dramatically facilitates basal-to-luminal transition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Hypermethylation of the CpG shore, the upstream region with reduced CG density of the CpG island in the Shh promoter region, is responsible for the loss of Shh.
source: Our study reveals that hypermethylation of the CpG shore, the upstream region with a reduced CG density of the CpG island in the Shh promoter region, is responsible for the loss of Shh
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 1.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of DNA methylation with agents such as 5'-azacitidine induces increased expression of Shh, thereby halting the progression of urothelial carcinoma.
source: pharmacological inhibition of DNA methylation with agents such as 5'-azacitidine induces increased expression of Shh, thereby halting the progression of urothelial carcinoma
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The CpG shore regions, rather than CpG islands, of genes involved in tumorigenesis are important.
source: These findings are supported by other studies that show the importance of the CpG shore regions, rather than CpG islands, of genes involved in tumorigenesis (Ellis et al., 2009; Irizarry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A previous TCGA analysis showed frequent mutations in methyltransferases and demethylases, such as MLL2, ARID1A, and KDM6A.
source: A previous TCGA analysis showed frequent mutations in methyltransferases and demethylases, such as MLL2, ARID1A, and KDM6A
evidence: This is based on citation to TCGA analysis.

claim: The increased Shh methylation may be due to mutations in genes associated with epigenetic regulation such as MLL2, ARID1A, and KDM6A.
source: raising the interesting possibility that the increased Shh methylation is due to the mutations in these genes associated with epigenetic regulation
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The complex enhancer of the Shh gene is a cluster of three long-range, 840 kb regions.
source: whether the complex enhancer of the Shh gene, a cluster of three long-range, 840 kb regions (Lettice et al., 2003; Sagai et al., 2009), is associated with the development of urothelial carcinoma
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tumors exhibit a great degree of plasticity.
source: However, recent advances in cancer biology and genomics have modified this traditional view, demonstrating that cancer is not a single-factorial genetic disease and that tumors exhibit a great degree of plasticity.
evidence: This is a general statement about current understanding in cancer biology.

claim: The tumor subtypes are epigenetically switched through dynamic interactions with the tumor stroma mediated by Hh-BMP signaling feedback.
source: Our observation that the tumor subtypes are epigenetically switched through the dynamic interactions with the tumor stroma—mediated by Hh-BMP signaling feedback—provides a clear basis for this recent view regarding tumor plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In the normal bladder, the development and regeneration of the urothelium depend on balanced proliferation of basal stem cells and their differentiation into luminal cells, controlled by stromal production of multiple factors.
source: In the normal bladder, our previous study has indicated that the development and regeneration of the urothelium depend on the balanced proliferation of basal stem cells and their differentiation into luminal cells, which is controlled by the stromal production of multiple factors (Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In bladder tumors, the hierarchical relationship between basal stem cells and luminal cells observed in the normal bladder is maintained as basal subtype is converted into luminal subtype.
source: It is interesting to speculate that in cases of bladder tumors, the hierarchical relationship between basal stem cells and luminal cells observed in the normal bladder is maintained as basal subtype is converted into luminal subtype of bladder cancer.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their findings.

claim: All luminal-like tumors induced by 5'-azacitidine treatment do not show histological features of the basal subtype.
source: Interestingly, all luminal-like tumors induced by 5'-azacitidine treatment in our study do not show histological features of the basal subtype (e.g. squamous differentiation), although some luminal-like tumors still maintain the low expression of certain basal markers.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: There may be an intermediate subtype between basal and luminal human bladder cancer, similar to intermediate cells in the urothelium of the normal bladder.
source: This suggests the interesting possibility that there may be the intermediate subtype between basal and luminal human bladder cancer, similar to the intermediate cells in the urothelium of the normal bladder.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Suppressing Hh-BMP feedback signaling with individual shRNAs for Shh or Bmpr1a along with 5'-azacitidine treatment was insufficient to regain the gene expression of the strong basal signature.
source: Moreover, in our rescue experiment, we noticed that suppressing Hh-BMP feedback signaling with individual shRNAs for Shh or Bmpr1a along with 5'-azacitidine treatment was insufficient to regain the gene expression of the strong basal signature based on the GSEA analyses (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G)
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5D, 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Additional mechanisms regulated by DNA methylation—other than Hh-BMP feedback signaling—may be involved to support the complete conversion of bladder tumors into the luminal subtype.
source: These data imply the potential involvement of additional mechanisms regulated by DNA methylation—other than Hh-BMP feedback signaling—to support the complete conversion of bladder tumors into the luminal subtype, particularly the complete loss of the basal signature
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The tissue dynamics of normal urothelium are controlled by multiple stromal factors such as Wnt, Fgf, and Bmp.
source: because the tissue dynamics of normal urothelium are controlled by multiple stromal factors such as Wnt, Fgf, and Bmp (Shin et al., 2011; Shin et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Early detection and prevention are important therapeutic options for the treatment of cancers.
source: Early detection and prevention are important therapeutic options for the treatment of cancers (Tomasetti et al., 2017; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation with 5'-azacitidine to increase Shh expression could have a potentially beneficial impact on the clinical management of human bladder cancer, especially at the early stage of onset or recurrence.
source: Pharmacological manipulation with 5'-azacitidine to increase Shh expression, resulting in therapeutic activation of stromal Bmp to block bladder tumor initiation through the differentiating of premalignant cells, could have a potentially beneficial impact on the clinical management of human bladder cancer, especially at the early stage of onset or recurrence
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication based on the study findings.

claim: The tumor-restraining effects of the stromal Hh response induced with pharmacological agents in full-fledged tumors carry significant therapeutic implications, especially for patients with late-stage invasive urothelial carcinoma.
source: In addition to clinical benefits in terms of cancer prevention, our findings regarding the tumor-restraining effects of the stromal Hh response induced with pharmacological agents in full-fledged tumors, carry significant therapeutic implications, especially for patients with late-stage of invasive urothelial carcinoma.
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication based on the study findings.

claim: A recent TCGA analysis revealed five different subtypes of muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma with different patient outcomes.
source: A recent TCGA analysis revealed five different subtypes of muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma with different patient outcomes (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014a; Choi et al., 2014; Hedegaard et al., 2016; Robertson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human invasive urothelial carcinomas were subdivided into five distinct molecular subtypes: luminal-papillary, luminal-infiltrated, luminal, basal and neuronal.
source: In these works, human invasive urothelial carcinomas were subdivided into five distinct molecular subtypes: luminal-papillary, luminal-infiltrated, luminal, basal and neuronal.
evidence: This is based on cited TCGA studies.

claim: The loss of Shh induced by DNA methylation of the CpG shore of the Shh promoter region leads to the initiation and growth of the basal subtype of urothelial carcinoma.
source: Our results show that the loss of Shh induced by DNA methylation of the CpG shore of the Shh promoter region leads to the initiation and, ultimately, growth of the basal subtype of urothelial carcinoma.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: With pharmacological induction of Shh expression in epithelial tumor cells of the basal subtype, urothelial carcinoma develops into a less aggressive, more manageable luminal-like subtype through stromally produced Bmp-mediated cellular differentiation.
source: With pharmacological induction of the expression of Shh in epithelial tumor cells of the basal subtype, which in turn increases the stromal Hh response, urothelial carcinoma develops into a less aggressive, more manageable luminal-like subtype of bladder cancer through stromally produced Bmp-mediated cellular differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The luminal subtype of urothelial carcinoma appears to grow more slowly, to be associated with better patient outcomes and to be more susceptible to the immune system than the basal subtype.
source: The luminal subtype of urothelial carcinoma appears to grow more slowly, to be associated with better patient outcomes and to be more susceptible to the immune system than the basal subtype (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: A recent study showed a phenotypic shift of luminal parental tumors to basal subtypes in patient-derived organoid culture, and this change is reversed in organoid xenografts where the tumor stroma is restored.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed a phenotypic shift of luminal parental tumors to basal subtypes in patient-derived organoid culture, and showed that this change is reversed in organoid xenografts in which the tumor stroma is restored (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The ability to convert molecular subtypes by modulation of Hh signaling with pharmacological agents could facilitate the development of personalized therapeutic options for urothelial carcinoma.
source: The ability to convert molecular subtypes by modulation of Hh signaling with pharmacological agents such as 5'-azacitidine could therefore facilitate the development of personalized therapeutic options for urothelial carcinoma and permit potential combinatorial therapy.
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication based on the study findings.

claim: Treatment with 5'-azacitidine and/or FK506 to activate the Hh response-induced expression of cellular differentiation factors in the tumor stroma would induce the luminal-like subtype, which is more manageable with subsequent treatment, including immunotherapy.
source: For example, treatment with 5'-azacitidine and/or FK506 (Shin et al., 2014b; Spiekerkoetter et al., 2013) to activate the Hh response-induced expression of cellular differentiation factors, such as BMPs, in the tumor stroma would induce the luminal-like subtype, which is more manageable with subsequent treatment, including immunotherapy (Massard et al., 2016; Powles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a therapeutic strategy proposed based on the study findings and supported by citations.

claim: Non-muscle-invasive carcinoma is derived from Shh-positive basal epithelial cells via a papillary pathway by maintaining active Hh signaling.
source: Non-muscle-invasive carcinoma, for example, is derived from Shh-positive basal epithelial cells, which have been previously identified as cells of origin of bladder cancer (Shin et al., 2014a), via a papillary pathway by maintaining active Hh signaling, in which Shh is expressed in the epithelium and the Hh response occurs in the stroma.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their model and supported by citation.

claim: The Hh response in the stroma induces the expression of secreted factors such as Wnts and Fgfs, which stimulate the proliferation of epithelial cells.
source: The Hh response in the stroma induces the expression of secreted factors such as Wnts and Fgfs, which in turn stimulate the proliferation of epithelial cells (Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Papillary invasive tumors develop with proliferative advantage of increased signaling feedback between epithelium and stroma and additional mutations of genes such as Fgfr3, while maintaining Shh expression and low CIS signatures.
source: With proliferative advantage of increased signaling feedback between the epithelium and stroma and the additional mutations of genes such as Fgfr3, papillary invasive tumors develop while maintaining Shh expression and low CIS signatures.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors as part of their proposed model.

claim: The luminal–infiltrated subtype follows the papillary lineage but accumulates mutations associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) while maintaining a moderate level of Shh expression and showing no mutations in p53.
source: The luminal–infiltrated subtype also follows the papillary lineage, but rather than mutations in Fgfr3, it accumulates mutations associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) while maintaining a moderate level of Shh expression and showing no mutations in p53.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors as part of their proposed model.

claim: The neuronal subtype may originate from neuroendocrine cells, not basal stem cells, and may develop in an Hh signaling-independent way.
source: Finally, the neuronal subtype characterized by the expression of neuroendocrine and neuronal genes (Sjödahl et al., 2017) may originate from neuroendocrine cells, but not basal stem cells, and may develop in an Hh signaling-independent way.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their analysis and supported by citation.
